item.title: Revenue Growth and Staff Expense: A Public-Company Follow-Up to Eclipse of Rent-Sharing
item.description: arXiv:2610.23869v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Does a widening gap between company revenue and staff expense per employee provide evidence of declining rent-sharing? We examine how reporting selection and sector composition affect that inference, as a follow-up to Acemoglu, He, and le Maire's Eclipse of Rent-Sharing. We assemble 7,000 company-years for 695 firms over 2015-2025. In a fixed sample of 75 staff-expense reporters, nominal revenue per employee rises 83.6%, while staff expense per employee rises 51.0%. The pooled expense-to-revenue ratio falls, but the pattern is concentrated in financial firms; among the other 25 reporters, aggregate staff expense per employee grows slightly faster than aggregate revenue per employee. These accounting measures identify neither real productivity nor the allocation of its gains between labor and capital. A separate audit of the original paper's reported estimates finds that some US output effects remain imprecisely estimated, while several Danish estimates support tighter bounds. The fitted reporting-probability model exhibits concentrated weights, substantial two-group imbalance and sectors without reporters; it does not justify generalizing payroll results. We extend the original study's measurement discussion to public-company accounts and qualify a blanket interpretation of no output effects: precision varies across its estimates. Our sector-dependent accounting results neither confirm nor overturn its causal wage and labor-share findings.
item.dc:creator: Haochuan Wang

item.title: TRACE: Governing AI-Assisted Research with Principles from Computer Science
item.description: arXiv:2610.24035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) makes it easier than ever to produce research outputs. The pressing question is how researchers should organize their work with this technology. The question is not new: software engineering and security research have long studied how teams of people and machines keep control of a shared body of work with many contributors. We distil principles from the practices these literatures report and transpose them to AI-assisted research. The principles form TRACE: Track records, Review against sources, Accept independently, Control transitions, and Evaluate corrections. Together, the five principles give researchers a common basis for remaining in control while integrating AI into their workflows. By bounding units of work and attending to how each is shaped, they help researchers pace AI-assisted work to human attention rather than to the speed at which AI produces content. We also introduce TRACE-OS, an open source operating system for AI-assisted research projects. It puts the principles into practice through shared instructions, tools, and records that fit researchers' existing workflows. The shared standard can contribute to building trust, which allows teams to delegate and realize the productivity that AI promises. More broadly, we aim to open a conversation about the governing principles through which the research community can benefit from AI.
item.dc:creator: Amirhossein Zohrehvand, Aldona Kapa\v{c}inskait\.{e}

item.title: The wealth-to-salary ratio: a simple indicator of inequality
item.description: arXiv:2610.24192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In previous studies, using agent-based simulations of a model of a capitalist economy proposed by Ian Wright, we showed that inequality in both wealth and income distributions is largely governed by a single key parameter: the ratio between average wealth per capita and the mean salary, denoted by $R$. This parameter captures the relative importance of accumulated assets compared with labor income. In the model, larger values of $R$ are systematically associated with higher levels of inequality, as measured by the Gini coefficient. In the present work, we investigate whether this relationship is also observed in real-world economies. Using empirical data from the World Inequality Database (WID) and the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), we construct empirical estimates of $R$ and compare them with standard measures of income and wealth inequality. We find a positive relation between $R$ and inequality across several empirical settings, with the strongest relationships observed for mature and advanced economies. These results provide empirical support for the role of the wealth-to-salary ratio as a simple macroscopic indicator associated with economic inequality, while also highlighting the limitations imposed by differences in data definitions and measurement across countries and periods.
item.dc:creator: Jhordan Silveira de Borba, Sebastian Gon\c{c}alves, Celia Anteneodo

item.title: When Better Opportunities Backfire: Service Worker Responses to Parallel AI Deployment in Customer Acquisition
item.description: arXiv:2610.25603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI voice agents get deployed in high-volume contact centers, firms can route low-intent leads to AI and allocate high-intent leads to human workers. Drawing on sequential search theory, we posit that AI-induced task allocation reshapes work, enriching opportunities facing human workers but also raising their reservation value for continuing with the lead in hand, making them less willing to persist. We study the effects of an AI voice-agent deployment at a Chinese online health-insurance brokerage using more than a half million customer outreach records surrounding the rollout. Adopting a regression-discontinuity-in-time design, we trace how worker behavior changes across the workday. Results show that the enrichment of human-facing opportunities concentrates early in the workday, raising the probability that a call is a high-intent lead by about 23 percentage points on the first three calls and fading to zero later. However, customer acquisition by human workers declines precisely where the enrichment is greatest, falling about 5 percentage points on the first three calls and flattening over the day. Consistent with the theorized reservation value mechanism, workers reallocate their earliest leads about 8 percentage points more often and persist less with them, shortening those calls by about 13%. A calibrated decomposition analysis further shows that the modest gain from improved lead ordering is outweighed by a much larger negative behavioral response. By reshaping the quality and within-workday distribution of opportunities, parallel AI deployment alters how workers pursue tasks, highlighting opportunity distribution as an important service operations state variable beyond workload and congestion.
item.dc:creator: Xinyu Fu, Shulong Luo, Narayan Ramasubbu, Peng Shen, Xincheng Wang, Yucheng Wang

item.title: How exposed is work to robotics? Occupational, industry, and geographic measures
item.description: arXiv:2610.24267v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Exposure indices that map technical capabilities onto occupational abilities have become a standard tool for anticipating how AI may reshape work, but existing measures either cover software AI or proxy robotics through patents and installation data that reflect the industrial robots of past decades. We construct the first abilities-based exposure measures for robotics and physical AI, and the first to span occupations, industries, and geographies. Following the framework of Felten et al. (2018, 2021), we build a robotics capability taxonomy of 16 capabilities in eight domains from 78 academic, industry, and standards sources, use a large language model to score the relatedness of each capability to the 52 ONET work abilities, and aggregate to Robotics Occupational Exposure (ROE) for 774 occupations, Robotics Industry Exposure (RIE) for 250 NAICS industries, and county-level Robotics Geographic Exposure (RGE). We find that robotics exposure concentrates in physically intensive work such as construction, farming, transportation, and production, and in industries such as logging, mining, trucking, and warehousing. Unlike generative-AI exposure, ROE is higher in occupations with lower wages, lower education requirements, and less creative-ability content. Physical collaboration and assistance, terrain-based locomotion, grasping and handling, and task and functional reasoning move the exposure ranking most, yet no single capability carries the index. Because the measures capture technical relatedness rather than readiness, cost, or adoption, they should be read as an upper bound on where physical automation could affect work.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Sartor, Robert Seamans, Neil Thompson

item.title: Strategic Origins of Network Structure
item.description: arXiv:2610.24792v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why specific mesoscale structures emerge remains elusive. Here we introduce the game-graph equilibrium, the stable rest point of a payoff-driven partner-choice dynamic, analogous to a Nash equilibrium. This reveals network structure as the fossilized record of strategic interaction. We prove analytically that two-type games have exactly four network topologies, which are their exhaustive thermodynamic phases: assortative, disassortative, and two core-peripheries. This result generalizes to $K^K$ topological classes for $K$-type interactions. Furthermore, four distinct Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies, yet their payoffs reveal whether the underlying dynamic is cooperative or exploitative. To recover the generating dynamics from observed networks, we develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to lie on a low-dimensional, game-theoretic manifold. Applied to real-world networks, the model yields interpretable quantities, distinguishes states that look identical to conventional methods, predicts network topologies it has never seen without retraining, and controls its own complexity without hand-tuned penalties. Networks such as international trade are well described by the model despite the hard constraint, suggesting that real-world systems are organized by payoff-driven partner choice. Our framework resolves a foundational ambiguity by offering a precise, mechanistic definition of communities: strategic equivalence.
item.dc:creator: Christoph Riedl, Rory Smead

item.title: Belief Bias Identification
item.description: arXiv:2404.09297v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper proposes a unified theoretical model to identify and test a comprehensive set of probabilistic updating biases within a single framework. The model achieves separate identification by focusing on the updating of belief distributions, rather than point beliefs alone. Estimating the model in a laboratory experiment reveals significant individual heterogeneity, with the hot-hand fallacy emerging as the most common bias and a key driver of biased inference. Accounting for additional distortions reveals associations across bias families and reduces the apparent prevalence of overinference and preference-based biases. At the population level, most biases average out, but base-rate neglect remains present.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Gonzalez-Fernandez

item.title: Time is Knowledge: Response Times in Binary Response Models
item.description: arXiv:2408.14872v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Response times contain information about economically relevant but unobserved variables like willingness to pay, preference intensity, quality, or happiness. We provide a general characterization of the properties of latent variables that can be detected using response time data. Our theoretical framework unifies and generalizes existing results in the literature and gives rise to many new applications. We illustrate the novel insights that the method can deliver through three empirical applications: identifying an optimal nudge, testing decreasing marginal happiness of income, and predicting treatment heterogeneity.
item.dc:creator: Jean-Michel Benkert, Shuo Liu, Nick Netzer

item.title: Work that Counts, and Work that Doesn't: Labor Supply in Experiments and Real Work
item.description: arXiv:2605.29832v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Do workers behave the same in experiments as they do in real life? Combining a real-effort emoji-counting experiment with platform records, self-reported expectations and recalls, and smartphone screen-time logs, we compare how the same workers on Prolific respond to randomized wage changes in the experiment and to wage variation in their actual work. Our results reveal that workers' behavior in experiments is remarkably different from real life. In the observational window, in fact, workers respond to expected wage changes just as they do in the experiment, but are much less responsive to unanticipated changes. However, once we condition on recall error in self-reports, we find that behavior in the two windows aligns. Recall error is then both a source of error for self-reported data but also the result of a process of inattention that affects effort itself, as unexpected wage changes often pass unnoticed.
item.dc:creator: Mattia Adamo, Michele Cantarella

item.title: Human Responses to Algorithmic Correction: Evidence from Centre Court
item.description: arXiv:2401.16754v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study how algorithmic review changes the initial decisions that a system is designed to correct. Using Hawk-Eye data from professional tennis, we compare umpire decisions with and without review against a common accuracy benchmark. Under review, initial errors were 8.6 percentage points higher just outside the line and lower for comparably close balls inside. We find no evidence that average initial accuracy deteriorated. Within matches, reversals were followed by larger adjustments than upheld calls, consistent with adaptation to correction. Overall, correction offsets worse initial decisions for incorrect in calls and reinforces better initial decisions for incorrect out calls. Whether review lowers organizational costs depends jointly on these changes and the costs of remedying corrected errors. A conditional illustration shows how utilization spreads fixed review costs across calls.
item.dc:creator: David Almog, Romain Gauriot, Lionel Page, Daniel Martin

item.title: Robustness over efficiency in climate coalitions: a bistable model and a map of architectures
item.description: arXiv:2608.12143v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Designs for international climate cooperation face a trade-off between efficiency and robustness to institutional erosion. We formalize it in a stylized coalition-formation game with two enrolment channels, a membership premium read as the value of club goods and an outsider drain, stabilized with robust control. The free-rider gap is exact within the game, measurable, and separated from the architecture-specific channels. The drain decomposes into a border channel, capped by trade law at the rent it mirrors, and a compensated world-market channel. With sufficiently strong channels the model is bistable, a remnant club and a near-universal coalition separated by a critical mass. For a proposed carbon currency, whose units are reissued each period, extinguished upon use, and enforced at the border, the minimal nucleus is thirty per cent of global emissions, ignition from an EU-China nucleus requires compensating one fifth to three fifths of the outsiders' world-market loss, the established coalition withstands two to four times the erosion admissible at ignition, and the tipping survives heterogeneity to three times the premium. Two robustness coordinates place each architecture on a map with three regimes: the carbon currency is self-igniting, the border adjustment founding-dependent, the export rebate permanent-support-dependent. A third coordinate, the coalition size up to which outsiders' border payments cover joiners' compensation, marks where the full coalition comes to rest on an internal transfer. Architectures without a drain improve efficiency within a coalition but cannot form one. Robustness governs whether cooperation forms and endures; efficiency decides how much an established coalition delivers.
item.dc:creator: Juergen Renn (Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, Jena, Germany)

item.title: Allocative Efficiency and the Returns to Innovation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14969v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Innovation changes welfare by improving technology and reallocating inputs across producers with different markups. When producers choose markups optimally, an innovator's own output and price adjustments have no private value at the margin, so reallocation affects its profit only through others' responses. For an innovator small in its markets, the change in allocative efficiency is of the same order as its cost saving but does not reach its profit. A process innovator is paid its cost saving, forgoing its own and downstream markups on added output. For U.S. public firms in 2015, these forgone markups average 26 percent of that saving. For innovators accounting for 56 percent of sales, allocative efficiency rises or falls by more than a tenth of their private return. With estimated spillovers, patenting firms' R&D has a social return 6.24 times its private return.
item.dc:creator: Koki Okumura

item.title: Market Efficiency in a Changing Asset Population: Mobility, Entry, and Survival over Cryptocurrency's Full History
item.description: arXiv:2610.23283v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Weak-form efficiency implies symmetry restrictions on the Markov chain governing movement across the cryptocurrency capitalisation distribution. We test them on the full listed population: 8,970 assets, 690 weekly cross-sections, 2013 to 2026, with entry, exit and survival observed rather than inferred. Symmetry is rejected in every era, but the asymmetry falls by seventy percent, and what converged is entry-driven compositional churn rather than coins' own valuations. The bottom decile earns 27.5% per week on paper and nothing among assets that trade, on capacity of $293,000. Compensation for neglect exists precisely where trading does not.
item.dc:creator: Antonis Ballis, Christos Ioannidis
